name: source-map (mozilla/source-map, Rust/WebAssembly mappings parser)
language: JavaScript with Rust compiled to WebAssembly (wasm-mappings)
baseline: source-map 0.6 pure-JavaScript source map parser (the same library before the Rust/wasm rewrite of the mappings parser)
workload: Parsing and querying real-world source maps in the library's own benchmark page (bench/bench.html), Rust-to-WebAssembly mappings parser versus the previous JavaScript parser.
claimed_speedup: Up to 5.89x faster than the JavaScript implementation on realistic benchmarks over real-world source maps (Mozilla Hacks, Jan 2018); editor note on the same post: later algorithmic improvements give up to 10.9x total over the original (both figures from a search-result snippet).
stars_or_usage: 3.7k stars; the wasm parser ships in source-map 0.7+, widely used by JS tooling
tradeoffs: Consumers must load lib/mappings.wasm (URL or ArrayBuffer passed to SourceMapConsumer.initialize), initialization is async, and each consumer must be freed manually with destroy() because wasm memory is not garbage collected; adds a .wasm file to deployments.
caveats: Snippet only: hacks.mozilla.org is blocked in this environment, so the 5.89x and 10.9x figures were read from a web-search result snippet and the page was not opened. The repo's bench/ harness is a browser page with no recorded hardware or flags. A follow-up by Vyacheslav Egorov (mraleph) and Nick Fitzgerald's 'Speed Without Wizardry' showed the JavaScript parser could be tuned to roughly match the Rust/wasm version, so the win is against the unoptimised 2018 JS code. Numbers are from 2018 browsers.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'rewrote JavaScript library in Rust compiled to WebAssembly times faster than the JavaScript version npm benchmark' -> Mozilla Hacks 'Oxidizing Source Maps with Rust and WebAssembly' (snippet); repo opened on github.com

compiler_and_flags: Full wasm build: emcc 6.0.0 (emsdk) src/lexer.c -Oz -flto -DLEXER_SIMD -D LEX_TS --no-entry -s STANDALONE_WASM=1; minimal build -DLEXER_MIN -Oz -flto -mcpu=mvp then wasm-opt; asm.js baseline built with fastcomp emscripten 1.40.1 -Oz --closure 1 (all from chompfile.toml); Node.js 26 for the benchmark
name: es-module-lexer
language: C compiled to WebAssembly (emcc) with a TypeScript/JavaScript wrapper
baseline: Acorn (fastest pure-JS parser, per the README) and the library's own CSP asm.js build of the same C lexer
workload: Lexing ECMAScript module import/export syntax over the 3.1 MB test/samples set (run via `chomp bench`, warm numbers averaged over 25 parses); README example: Angular 1 (720KiB) lexed in 1 ms.
claimed_speedup: Wasm build 4.7 ms/MB cold and 3.2 ms/MB warm versus the asm.js build of the same lexer at 14.9 / 6.3 ms/MB (3.2x cold, 2.0x warm, derived from page data); minimal build 4.5 / 3.1 versus 10.8 / 5.7 ms/MB. README: Angular 1 (720KiB) is fully lexed in 1 ms 'in comparison to the fastest JS parser, Acorn which takes over 100ms'.
stars_or_usage: 1.0k stars; used by es-module-shims and bundler/tooling pipelines
tradeoffs: Lexer only (imports/exports, no AST); full build needs WebAssembly SIMD (Chrome 91+, Firefox 89+, Safari 16.4+), the minimal build avoids SIMD; async init() before use; a CSP-safe asm.js build exists for environments that forbid wasm.
caveats: First-party numbers on an unnamed machine; the >100x comparison against Acorn compares a lexer with a full AST parser and the table itself contains no Acorn row; the wasm is built with -Oz (size) rather than -O3, so it is not tuned for speed. Wasm-versus-asm.js ratios are for the same C source, not for an independently written JS lexer.

name: zip.js (@zip.js/zip.js WebAssembly zlib codec)
language: JavaScript with bundled WebAssembly zlib and AES codecs
baseline: zip.js's own pure-JavaScript zlib port, jszip (pako) and fflate; also native CompressionStream and node:zlib shown for reference
workload: Compress/decompress 20 MB of compressible text, 20 MB incompressible data and 5,000 x ~2 KB text files in Node, each (library, operation, workload) in a fresh process, median of 3 runs.
claimed_speedup: Decompress 20 MB text: WASM zlib 71 ms vs pure-JS zlib 155 ms, jszip/pako 140 ms, fflate 116 ms. Compress 20 MB incompressible: WASM 460 ms vs pure-JS 787 ms, jszip 854 ms. Compress 20 MB text: WASM 1098 ms vs pure-JS 1229 ms, jszip 1753 ms. 5,000 small files compress: WASM 551 ms vs pure-JS 962 ms, jszip 846 ms. AES-256 (Node): WebAssembly 131 MB/s vs JavaScript 114 MB/s (page of release 2.15.0 via jsr.io).
tradeoffs: WASM module instantiation costs about 20 ms per fresh process; peak memory is higher than fflate (139 MB vs 68 MB delta on the 20 MB text compress); the codec is used only when native CompressionStream is unavailable or the wasm backend is configured.
caveats: The wasm backend is not the fastest option overall: native CompressionStream and node:zlib beat it (compress text 678-730 ms vs 1098 ms) and fflate beats it on incompressible data (298 ms) and on small files (278 ms compress, 101 ms decompress). The win is wasm versus the JS port of the same codec and versus pako. Author-run, machine-specific by the page's own warning; wasm build flags are not stated, which keeps this at C although the harness (benchmarks/), CPU and runtime versions are public.

name: Automerge (Rust core compiled to WebAssembly, 2.x)
language: Rust (WebAssembly build) with JavaScript bindings; also a C API
baseline: Automerge 0.14.1, the earlier pure-JavaScript implementation (Yjs 13.6.11 shown as the JS reference)
workload: crdt-benchmarks: B1.x text editing sequences of N=6000 operations in Node, e.g. append N characters (B1.1) and prepend N characters (B1.3), plus the real-world editing trace B4.
claimed_speedup: Derived from page data (two tables of the README, possibly different runs): B1.1 append 6000 chars 365 ms (Automerge 2.1.10, wasm) vs 2460 ms (0.14.1, JS) = 6.7x; B1.3 prepend 307 ms vs 83,488 ms = 272x. Relative to Yjs, Automerge went from 8.1x slower (2460 vs 303 ms) to 1.9x slower (365 vs 188 ms) on B1.1. Still slower than Yjs on B4 (14,326 ms vs 5,714 ms).
tradeoffs: Bundle 1,737,571 bytes (604,118 gzipped) versus Yjs 69,124 (20,100); smaller documents than Yjs (3,992 vs 6,031 bytes on B1.1); suite's memUsed does not include wasm runtime memory.
caveats: The comparison is the project against its own predecessor, taken from two separate tables in the README (older table: Automerge 0.14.1 and Yjs 13.3.0; current table: Automerge 2.1.10 and Yjs 13.6.11) so absolute ratios mix runs; the suite is maintained by the Yjs author; Automerge is still slower than Yjs in the current table; the README notes Automerge does B4 in about 1 s if all changes are applied in a single change() transaction.

name: ywasm (y-crdt, Rust port of Yjs compiled to WebAssembly)
workload: crdt-benchmarks text editing at N=6000 in Node: B1.1 append, B1.3 prepend, B1.4 random inserts, B2.4 concurrent insert/delete, B4 real-world editing trace.

caveats: Mixed result, not an overall win: ywasm is 5x slower than Yjs on the real-world trace and on concurrent edits. Kept as the wasm library of record for the shootout; the numbers come from a suite written by the Yjs author. memUsed shows 0 B for wasm because it excludes wasm memory.

name: blake3 (connor4312/blake3, BLAKE3 for JavaScript)
language: Rust compiled to WebAssembly plus a Node native binding, with TypeScript wrapper
baseline: Node.js built-in md5, sha1 and sha256 hashing (the README does not say whether the md5/sha rows are Node crypto or pure JS)
workload: Hashing 64 B, 64 KB and 6 MB buffers in Node 12 with the matcha benchmark (benchmark.js).
claimed_speedup: README: 'Blake3 is significantly faster than Node's built-in hashing.' 64 B: blake3 wasm 1,040,000 ops/s vs md5 276,000, sha1 263,000, sha256 271,000 (about 3.8-4.0x, derived from page data); 64 KB: wasm 6,410 ops/s vs sha1 13,900, md5 9,900, sha256 6,470 (not faster); 6 MB: wasm 65.2 vs md5 106, sha1 150, sha256 69.2 (slower), native binding 502 ops/s.
tradeoffs: The wasm build only wins on tiny inputs, where per-call overhead dominates; large-input speed needs the native Node binding, which the README calls a work in progress.
caveats: Mixed: the wasm module is slower than the built-in hashes from 64 KB upward, and the headline claim is carried by the native binding. Node 12 numbers on an unnamed laptop; the md5/sha rows are not described. Included to document the wasm trade-off, not as a clear win.

name: fast-md5-web
language: Rust compiled to WebAssembly with a TypeScript Web Worker pool
workload: Browser MD5 of large files and batches, single-thread wasm and multi-thread worker pool, against spark-md5.
claimed_speedup: README: about 8x faster than spark-md5 in single-thread mode and about 16x faster with multi-thread workers ('in specific scenarios'; 'up to 16x faster for large files').
tradeoffs: Worker pool and SharedArrayBuffer path (cross-origin isolation headers) give the 16x; ESM-only package; MD5 is not collision resistant.
caveats: The README gives ratios only plus a result screenshot (docs/a3d25c4789...png) and a demo page; no hardware, browser, file sizes or timings in text. The 16x figure includes multi-threading versus single-threaded spark-md5, so it is not a per-core comparison. The README calls it 'possibly the fastest'.

baseline: txml, xml-js, fast-xml-parser and xml2js (pure-JavaScript XML to JSON converters)
